hint.p: Near that point the upper half is a graph. As x changes a little, y must change so that the point stays on the curve.

note.title: Implicit differentiation
note.p: When an equation relates x and y, and y is treated as a differentiable function of x, differentiate both sides with respect to x. Every time a derivative falls on y, use the chain rule.

subsection.title: The chain rule is doing the hidden work
subsection.p: Implicit differentiation can feel like a new trick, but it is only the chain rule applied carefully.
The first term comes from differentiating x^2. The second term comes from differentiating y^3, which requires the chain rule.

hint.p: The expression y^2 is really (y(x))^2. Differentiating a composite produces the inside derivative y'.

subsection.title: When the method warns us
subsection.p: Implicit differentiation assumes that near the point we care about, the curve can be treated as one differentiable function y(x). The equation itself does not always guarantee that.

paragraphs.title: A vertical tangent
paragraphs.p: No finite value of y' can satisfy this equation. That does not mean the circle has no tangent. It means the tangent is vertical, so its slope dy/dx is not a finite number.
The point (5,0) is also where the upper and lower branches meet at the right edge. Near that point, the circle cannot be written as a differentiable function y(x) with a finite derivative.

paragraphs.title: A relation with two branches
paragraphs.p: At (0,0), both branches meet. If we choose the branch y=x, the slope is 1. If we choose the branch y=-x, the slope is -1.
which does not determine y'. The reason is geometric: the equation has not selected one branch.

warning.title: Implicit differentiation warning
warning.p: When the equation does not define one smooth branch y(x) near the point, the algebra may produce no slope, many possible slopes, or an equation that does not determine dy/dx.

paragraphs.p: These warnings are useful. They do not break the method. They tell us what the geometry is doing.

exercise.title: When does the algebra warn that there is no finite y'?

statement.p: At (5,0) on the circle, the differentiated equation cannot be solved for a finite slope; at the origin of y^2=x^2, it becomes 0=0. In your own words, what is the geometry doing in each case, and why is that a warning rather than a broken method?

hint.p: A vertical tangent has no finite dy/dx. Two branches meeting at a point have not selected one function y(x).

subsection.title: What implicit differentiation gives us
subsection.p: Implicit differentiation turns an equation into slope information.
In each case, the slope may depend on both coordinates. That is natural: a point on a curve has both an x-coordinate and a y-coordinate, and the tangent direction depends on where the point lies.

note.title: Main idea
note.p: Implicit differentiation avoids solving for y. It uses the chain rule to differentiate the relation directly, then solves for dy/dx.

subsection.p: The chain rule and implicit differentiation now let us handle complicated algebraic layers and many curves. But some of the most important functions in calculus are not algebraic. The next step is periodic motion: sine, cosine, and the derivatives that make waves and rotation calculable.

exercise.title: Why may the slope depend on both x and y?

statement.p: Implicit differentiation often produces a formula for y' that still involves y. In your own words, why is that natural for a curve, rather than a defect of the method?

hint.p: A point on a curve has two coordinates. The tangent direction can depend on where the point sits, not only on its x-coordinate.
